concept.name: Uncovered interest parity
concept.definition: The hypothesis that the interest rate differential between two currencies equals the expected change in their exchange rate, so that the higher-yielding currency is expected to depreciate just enough to offset its yield advantage for an unhedged investor. Empirically UIP fails: high-interest-rate currencies tend to appreciate rather than depreciate, a puzzle that underlies carry-trade profitability.
concept.intuition: UIP says there's no free lunch from chasing higher foreign interest rates — the exchange rate should move to cancel the extra yield. In practice it often doesn't.
concept.mechanics: Unlike covered parity, UIP cannot be enforced by arbitrage because the future spot rate is unknown; it is a joint hypothesis about expectations and risk neutrality. Research links its failure to funding-liquidity constraints on carry traders: exchange-rate moves between high- and low-rate currencies are negatively skewed, and controlling for liquidity helps explain the uncovered interest-rate puzzle.
concept.formula: E[S_T] / S = (1 + r_q x T) / (1 + r_b x T), equivalently the expected percentage change in the spot rate ~= r_b - r_q over the tenor; S = spot in quote per base currency.
concept.failure_modes: UIP fails systematically (the forward premium puzzle): since the 1990s high-rate currencies characteristically appreciated, so unhedged carry positions earned excess returns punctuated by crash episodes when funding liquidity dried up.
concept.misconceptions: UIP is not an arbitrage condition that 'must' hold — it is a falsifiable expectations hypothesis, and treating the forward rate as an unbiased forecast of the future spot rate is empirically wrong.
concept.example: If Australian rates exceed Japanese rates by 4%, UIP predicts the AUD should depreciate about 4% against the JPY over the year; historically AUD/JPY instead appreciated for long stretches, rewarding carry traders until sharp reversals.

citations.source: NBER Working Paper 14473 — Carry Trades and Currency Crashes (Brunnermeier, Nagel, Pedersen)
